instructions: Ensure every Excel model is delivered with ZERO formula errors (#REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, #N/A, #NAME?).
When modifying existing templates, study and exactly match the existing format, style, and conventions; never impose standardized formatting on files with established patterns.

Apply industry-standard color coding conventions unless otherwise stated by the user or existing template: use blue text (RGB: 0,0,255) for hardcoded inputs and scenario numbers, black text (RGB: 0,0,0) for all formulas and calculations, green text (RGB: 0,128,0) for links pulling from other worksheets within the same workbook, red text (RGB: 255,0,0) for external links to other files, and yellow background (RGB: 255,255,0) for key assumptions needing attention or cells that need to be updated.
Format years as text strings (e.g., '2024' not '2,024').
Use $#,##0 format for currency and always specify units in headers (e.g., 'Revenue ($mm)').
Use number formatting to make all zeros display as '-', including percentages (e.g., '$#,##0;($#,##0);-').
Default percentages to 0.0% format (one decimal).
Format multiples as 0.0x for valuation multiples (EV/EBITDA, P/E).
Use parentheses for negative numbers, e.g., (123) not -123.

Place ALL assumptions (growth rates, margins, multiples, etc.) in separate assumption cells and use cell references instead of hardcoded values in formulas; for example, use =B5*(1+$B$6) instead of =B5*1.05.

Verify all cell references are correct, check for off-by-one errors in ranges, ensure consistent formulas across all projection periods, test with edge cases (zero values, negative numbers), and verify no unintended circular references.
Document hardcoded values by adding a comment or text in cells beside them (if at end of table) with the format 'Source: [System/Document], [Date], [Specific Reference], [URL if applicable]'.
Use pandas for data analysis, visualization, and basic operations on Excel files.
Always use Excel formulas instead of calculating values in Python and hardcoding them; the spreadsheet should be able to recalculate when source data changes.
After creating or modifying an Excel file with formulas, recalculate formulas using the recalc.py script with the command 'python recalc.py output.xlsx'.
After recalculating, verify the output and fix any errors reported by the recalc.py script, including #REF!, #DIV/0!, #VALUE!, and #NAME? errors, then recalculate again.
When creating new Excel files, use openpyxl for formulas and formatting.
When editing existing Excel files, use openpyxl to preserve formulas and formatting.
Test 2-3 sample references to verify they pull correct values before building the full model.
Confirm Excel columns match correctly (e.g., column 64 = BL, not BK).
Remember Excel rows are 1-indexed (DataFrame row 5 = Excel row 6).
Check for null values with pd.notna() when handling NaN.
Check denominators before using '/' in formulas to avoid #DIV/0! errors.
Verify all cell references point to intended cells to avoid #REF! errors.
Use correct format (Sheet1!A1) for cross-sheet references when linking sheets.
Test formulas on 2-3 cells before applying broadly.
Check all cells referenced in formulas exist.
Test edge cases including zero, negative, and very large values.
Use pandas for data analysis, bulk operations, and simple data export; use openpyxl for complex formatting, formulas, and Excel-specific features.
When working with openpyxl, remember cell indices are 1-based (row=1, column=1 refers to cell A1).
Use data_only=True to read calculated values from an Excel file, but do not save the file when opened with data_only=True as formulas will be replaced with values and permanently lost.
For large files, use read_only=True for reading or write_only=True for writing with openpyxl.
When working with pandas, specify data types to avoid inference issues using dtype parameter, read specific columns with usecols, and handle dates properly with parse_dates.
Write minimal, concise Python code without unnecessary comments, verbose variable names, redundant operations, or unnecessary print statements.
Add comments to cells with complex formulas or important assumptions in Excel files.
Document data sources for hardcoded values in Excel files.
Include notes for key calculations and model sections in Excel files.
